new_statements.rule_in_words: Arandic-wide rule, applied to Antekerrepenh by inclusion rather than by a dedicated statement: primary stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant -- i.e. on the initial syllable of consonant-initial words and on the second syllable of vowel-initial words (most words are vowel-initial); onset-sensitive, otherwise fixed at the left edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Antekerrepenh. Koch 1997:279 only remarks historically that four-syllable words in many Australian languages carry penultimate secondary stress (pre-Arandic), not a synchronic Ant claim.
new_statements.exceptions: Breen 2001:56: Antekerrepenh (and Ayerrereng) pronounce a homorganic glide before word-initial /i/ or /u/, and one Ayerrereng speaker 'sometimes transferred the stress to this vowel' (possible change in progress). Breen 2001:53 (Central Arrernte): loss of the velar glide h leaves stress/length on the initial vowel (ahentye [a'ntje]), and younger CAr speakers shift stress to the initial vowel in surface VCV words. Blevins 2001:488 lists Antekerrepenh under 'Arandic (all with stress shift)', initial C-loss 'invariable', citing Hale 1962 and Koch 1997.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level main stress in citation forms; Breen frames the rule via VC(C) syllabification (Breen & Pensalfini 1999). No Antekerrepenh-specific stress sentence was found in any opened source; the dedicated primary description (Breen 1977 Phonetica; Breen 1982 IAD grammar ms) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Andegerebinha' (ande1247, ISO adg) = Antekerrepenh(e) (Austlang C12), the nearly extinct easternmost Arandic dialect (Breen 1977 'Andegerebenha'; Koch 'Ant'). Breen 2001 treats it as a dialect within the Arrernte group whose phonology is 'similar to that of CAr [Central Arrernte, east2379/cent2403 area]'. Hale's 1960 'Antikiripinhi (Georgina River variety)' material is per Breen 2001:56 fn.22 actually Ayerrereng (ayer1246), a closely related but distinct variety; do not conflate. The stress statements quoted are Arandic-wide (aran1267), not elicited specifically for ande1247.

sources.note: p.285 (SC10 'Stress shift to second syllable'): 'Stress in Arandic is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant (i.e. (V)'CV). This reflects the second syllable of Pre-Arandic.' Antekerrepenhe (Ant) is one of the Arandic varieties covered (abbreviations p.271; p.274 cites Breen 1977 for Ant prepalatalised apicals). Family-level synchronic generalisation in a historical paper, not an Ant-specific description.

sources.note: p.55: 'The most widespread stress rule in Arandic.. main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant.. stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.' Sec.4.1 (pp.55-56) on Antekerrepenh revises Breen 1977's vowel analysis and says 'Ant phonology is now regarded as similar to that of CAr [Central Arrernte]' but gives no separate Ant stress statement; p.56 (Ayerrereng) notes 'the Ant peculiarity of pronouncing a homorganic glide before initial /i/ or /u/' and that one Ayerrereng speaker 'sometimes transferred the stress to this vowel'.
